The simplest way to think about infelicity is this: it is the opposite of felicity. And felicity means two things — happiness, and a quality of being perfectly suited or well-chosen. So infelicity flips both of those:

  • It can mean unhappiness or misfortune.
  • More commonly, it means something that is awkward, inappropriate, or poorly chosen — especially a word, phrase, remark, or action that just doesn't fit the situation.

These two meanings are closely related. Think of it this way: when something is infelicitous, it creates a kind of discomfort — a feeling that something is off, that it doesn't belong, that it's the wrong choice for the moment. That sense of wrongness connects unhappiness and inappropriateness under one word.

In its more literary and old-fashioned sense, infelicity simply means a state of unhappiness, or a misfortune — something unfortunate that has happened to someone.

"He bore the infelicities of his early life with great dignity."

Here, "infelicities" means the hardships or unhappy circumstances he faced. This sense is mostly found in older writing, formal prose, or literature. In everyday modern speech, you are unlikely to use the word this way, but you may encounter it while reading classic texts.
Meaning 2: An Awkward or Inappropriate Expression, Remark, or Action (the dominant modern sense)

This is where infelicity really lives in modern usage, and this is the sense you will encounter most often.

An infelicity is something — usually a word, phrase, sentence, or social action — that is ill-suited to its context. It's not necessarily wrong in an absolute sense, but it is the wrong choice for the moment. It feels clumsy, misplaced, jarring, or inappropriate given the circumstances.

Think of it as a mismatch between what was said or done and what the situation actually called for.

In Language and Writing

Writers, editors, and critics use this word a great deal. When a piece of writing contains a phrase that feels clunky, a word that doesn't quite fit, or a sentence that strikes a false note, that is an infelicity of expression or simply a linguistic infelicity.

"The editor flagged several infelicities in the draft — phrases that were technically correct but felt awkward and out of place."

"Describing a funeral as a 'celebration of the end of someone's burden' was an infelicity that upset the family."

The word is especially useful because it captures something subtler than a plain error. An infelicity is often not a grammatical mistake or a factual error — it's more of a tonal mismatch, a clumsy choice, or a failure of judgment about what fits. A good writer might choose a technically correct word that is nonetheless an infelicity because it has the wrong tone for the context, or is too formal, too casual, too cold, or too vague for what the moment demands.

In Social Situations

An infelicity can also be a remark or action that is socially awkward or inappropriate — something said or done that makes people uncomfortable because it doesn't suit the situation.

"Mentioning his ex-wife's name during the wedding toast was a notable social infelicity."

"Her infelicity in choosing that moment to ask for a raise — right after her boss had delivered bad news to the whole team — did not go unnoticed."

Again, notice: it's not that these people did something monstrous. They just made a wrong-footed choice, a misstep in judgment about what was appropriate.

The plural form — infelicities — is extremely common and often used to describe a collection of small awkward flaws, particularly in a piece of writing or a speech.

"Overall the report was strong, though it contained a few infelicities that a good proofread would fix."

"His speech was memorable despite its infelicities."

You might wonder: why not just say mistake, awkwardness, or inappropriateness? Here's what infelicity adds that those words don't quite capture:

  • It suggests the problem is one of fit and judgment, not necessarily of technical rule-breaking.
  • It carries a tone that is measured and civilized — it is critical, but not brutal. Calling something an infelicity is a refined, restrained way of pointing out a flaw.
  • It implies the speaker or writer had a duty of care — a responsibility to choose more wisely — and fell short of it.

So when a critic or an editor or a careful reader says something is an infelicity, they are saying: "This was the wrong choice for this context, and a more thoughtful choice was available."

An awkward, inappropriate, or ill-chosen word, phrase, remark, or actionThe dominant modern sense. Something that doesn't suit its context — clumsy in tone, manner, or judgment.
One Final Way to Remember It

Here is a simple mental anchor: imagine a musician who plays the right notes but in completely the wrong style for the occasion — jazz at a classical recital, for instance. Nobody can say a rule was broken, but something is clearly off. That off-ness — that mismatch, that wrongness of fit — is the feeling that infelicity names.
